A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CAMEL study. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching; v2 primarily expands the appendix.

before.justification: v1 reports original CAMEL benchmark results, training and inference ablations, and confidence and self-correction analyses in Tables 1–2 and Figures 2, 4–7.

after.justification: v2 retains these original results and adds cross-model confidence analyses, threshold operating points, error-recovery measurements, and case studies in Appendix A.3–A.5.

M1.justification: The judging prompts, Algorithms 1–2, confidence gate, GRPO objective, binary reward, and counterfactual prefix augmentation remain unchanged. The additional base models are subjects of confidence analysis, not revisions to CAMEL.

E1.justification: Both versions use Skywork Reward Preference 80K, Code-Preference-Pairs, and Math-Step-DPO-10K for training, and RewardBench, RM-Bench, and JudgeBench for evaluation. The new analyses and examples use these existing datasets without introducing distinct task or input-environment coverage.

E2.justification: Comparator membership remains unchanged in Tables 1–2 and Figure 4, including the two RM-R1 models in the efficiency comparison. Appendix A.3 examines six additional base models' confidence signals rather than adding them as baselines against CAMEL.

E3.justification: Appendix A.3 substantially expands evaluation configurations through six additional base models across five existing datasets. Appendix A.4 adds confidence-partition error and recovery evaluation and threshold operating points across all three benchmarks, including JudgeBench. Section 4.3 also changes its illustrative threshold from 25 to 5; the original default threshold of 5 and training setup remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds extensive tests of confidence-signal generality across models, analysis of high-confidence errors and their recoverability, and six detailed success and failure cases. Threshold sensitivity analysis also extends to JudgeBench. These substantially expand the original ablations and aggregate confidence analyses.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run or seed information, statistical confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. The added density and binned-accuracy plots continue existing descriptive reporting practices; their confidence scores measure model verdict margins, not statistical uncertainty.

E6.justification: Tables 1–2 and the original plotted results are retained, while Figures 9–18 and Tables 3–10 add extensive numerical and qualitative findings. Table 3 newly reports forced-reflection recovery of 10/61, 385/877, and 8/48 high-confidence errors. Table 4 reports default-threshold accuracies of 94.2%, 84.9%, and 67.1%, conflicting with Table 1's retained 92.4%, 81.9%, and 69.1% for RewardBench, RM-Bench, and JudgeBench. Without an explained setting difference, these cannot establish version-to-version performance gains.

T1.justification: The mathematical formulation, confidence definition, gating equation, objective, and reward equations remain unchanged. No theoretical assumptions, propositions, or proofs are added; mathematical calculations in the new case studies are task examples.

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion retain the same methodological contributions, confidence-correctness claim, 82.9% average accuracy and 3.2-point advantage claims, and accuracy-efficiency Pareto claim. Additional appendix evidence does not redefine these core claims.

C2.justification: Appendix A.3–A.5 adds substantive interpretations of cross-model generality, benchmark-dependent threshold choices, and the limits of bypassing reflection. It distinguishes recoverable high-confidence errors from persistent over-refusal and style-preference failures. Table 2's caption also broadens its robustness wording from JudgeBench to all three benchmarks despite unchanged scores.

D1.justification: The new analyses specify base-model variants, concrete threshold settings of 3, 5, and 7, and offline forced-reflection handling for failure cases. Appendix A.4 adds validation-set guidance for selecting a threshold without specifying an actual validation split. Original training details, prompts, and resource-access information remain unchanged.

R1.justification: The related-work discussion and cited-work inventory are unchanged. The additional model analyses do not revise CAMEL's positioning relative to earlier reward-modeling or judging methods.

P1.justification: v2 makes limited introductory wording and cross-reference edits, expands Figure 7's explanation, replaces the preprint footer with conference information, and appends three organized subsections. The existing narrative and section order are largely preserved rather than extensively rewritten.

P2.justification: v2 adds ten multi-panel figures, two numerical tables, and six case-study tables with highlighted response and reflection passages. These substantially expand the visual presentation. Existing Figures 1–8 and Tables 1–2 remain, with limited caption edits and surrounding layout changes.

improvement.justification: The cross-model confidence checks and explicit failure analyses strengthen evidence for the routing signal and clarify limitations that v1 barely examines. However, new Table 4 contradicts the retained main results at the stated default threshold on all three benchmarks, without documenting different settings. These substantive benefits coexist with an unresolved reliability problem in the added accuracy-cost evidence, preventing a confident judgment of net overall improvement.
